## Reproducibility and analytical choice {#the-same-t-within-an-analyst}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Everyone who chose the same analyst got **the same *t***, to the third decimal, on different machines. That is reproducibility, and once the data and the code are in hand it is the cheap R.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The analysts did not get the same *t*: −3.804, −7.169 and −1.206, on one claim, under one set of instructions.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None was careless. The numbers differ because they made different choices about the **data** (which unemployment series, which respondents), the **model** (which fixed effects) and the **code** (one wave appended twice).
:::
::::

::: notes
Everyone who chose the same analyst arrived at the same number, to the third decimal, on different machines. [advance] Across the analysts, the values are minus three point eight, minus seven point two and minus one point two, for one claim, from analysts who received the same instructions. [advance] None of us was careless, and the numbers differ because of choices. On the data, KQXUE measured unemployment as a share of the whole population aged twenty to sixty-four rather than of the labour force, and left out the respondents who mentioned nothing, whom I scored zero. On the model, KQXUE has a fixed effect for each country and none for the year, where mine has both. On the code, the Stata script appended one wave twice, and my own first build read one wave twice too, an error that I corrected before the robustness study recorded my value, and choices of this kind are the subject of robustness, the second R.
:::

## Three models side by side {#three-models-side-by-side .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Analyst | Model | What it compares | Conventional *t* |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| C6HJR | fixed effects for country and year | each country with itself, after the change common to all countries in a year | −3.804 on 233 df |
| KQXUE | a fixed effect for each country | each country with itself, the common change included | −7.169 on 242 df |
| 018OL | random intercepts for country, year and wave | change within countries and differences between them at once | −1.206 on 396.9 df |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Between the 27 country means the slope is +`r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$b_between, 4)`, within countries `r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$b_within, 4)`: a model that blends the two comparisons, as random intercepts do, assumes them equal, and the within–between model rejects that (p = `r fmt_num(bw_cosmo$p_difference)`).
:::

::: {.src}
`data/display_between_within.csv`.
:::

::: notes
The three models reproduced by the class are the three estimators around which the menu is built. My model has fixed effects for country and for year, so that each country is compared with itself net of whatever all of Europe went through in a year. KQXUE has a fixed effect for each country only, which leaves the common change in the comparison, and 018OL has random intercepts for country, year and wave, which use the change within countries and the differences between them at once. [advance] On this panel the two comparisons point in opposite directions, since the slope across the country means is slightly positive and the slope within countries negative, and the within–between model rejects the equality that random intercepts assume. That difference is one reason why the three t-values lie so far apart, and the second half calls this decision the Estimator.
:::

## Twenty-seven clusters {#twenty-seven-clusters .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Test | Two-way fixed effects (C6HJR) | Country fixed effects, on the country-year panel |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Conventional | t = `r fmt_num(inference_of("conventional", "t"), 2)` on `r inference_of("conventional", "df")` df, p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("conventional", "p"), 4)` | t = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$t[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "conventional"], 2)` on `r disp_inference$df[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "conventional"]` df |
| Clustered by country, CR1 | t = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr1_g1", "t"), 2)` on 26 df, p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr1_g1", "p"), 3)` | t = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$t[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr1_g1"], 2)` on 26 df |
| Clustered, CR2, Satterthwaite df | t = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "t"), 2)` on `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "df"), 1)` df, p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)` | t = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$t[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], 2)` on `r fmt_num(disp_inference$df[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], 1)` df, p = `r fmt_num(disp_inference$p[disp_inference$estimator == "fe_country" & disp_inference$inference == "cr2_satterthwaite"], 4)` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The estimate is the same in every row; only the test changes. The years of one country are not independent, 27 countries are few clusters of unequal weight, and the CR2 test with Satterthwaite df, which classes every point of the curve, counts the countries that effectively carry the evidence.
:::

::: {.src}
@BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard; @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust; `data/display_inference.csv`.
:::

::: notes
Both reproduced t-values treat each row as independent evidence, although the years of one country resemble each other. Clustering by country allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and the evidence then rests on twenty-seven countries rather than two hundred and seventy rows. With so few clusters, of very unequal weight, the usual clustered test is still too generous, so the workshop uses the CR2 correction, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which count how many countries effectively carry the information, fewer than ten here. In my row, the same estimate goes from a p of two in ten thousand to just above point zero five, while the design of KQXUE, fitted on the country-year panel, stays significant under every test. [advance] The estimate is the same in every row and only the test changes, and the CR2 test is the one that classes every point of the curve.
:::
